newsitem.title: UK: Copper spikes higher, precious metals plunge.
newsitem.headline: Copper spikes higher, precious metals plunge.

text.p: Copper spiked to recent new heights on Tuesday and lifted the prices of other base metals but precious metals plunged to their lowest in years.
Copper, the London Metal Exchange's (LME) flagship contract, closed at $2,258, after hitting a six-month high of $2,285.
Many traders expect copper prices to reach $2,300 in the medium term. But gold fell to its lowest in almost two years while platinum plunged to a near three-year low.

In a special report on the copper market Bain and Co analysts Wiktor Bielski and Alan Williamson said prices were under levels that should prevail, based on a 15-year relationship between total reported stocks and prices.
"With the effects of the Sumitomo Corp scandal now fading, this discount is excessive and no longer justified," it said.
Copper's gains were helped by LME warehouse stocks falling 3,850 tonnes to 6-1/4 year lows of 90,050 tonnes, traders said.
Shortages of available metal for delivery to LME dealers' clients on some dates in December also provoked brisk business as the shortages forced dealers to pay premiums to meet their obligations.
Other base metals were quieter, but aluminium advanced to $1,535 on the back of an fall in LME warehouse inventory and Zinc hit an eight-month high and closed at $1,084.
In precious metals, gold slumped through the psychological barrier of $375 per ounce to fixed at $373.50, the lowest since January 1995.
Market sentiment has been largely bearish as investors shunned gold in favour of surging equities markets. Meanwhile, physical demand has remained lower than expected.

Some dealers said the fall could lure buyers at these prices and thus halt the slide, but they said if the $372 level was breached -- which would take gold back to prices not seen since April 1994 -- then a further plunge was likely.
"I think it's going to stabilise around here in the short term," a London-based dealer said.
Platinum fixed at the lowest point since December 1993 at $378.15 an ounce, driven downwards in the last few months by slack demand and ample supplies.
Silver and palladium were quieter.
In soft commodities, benchmark January coffee futures contract closed $16 down at $1,406, with all positions weaker.
Benchmark March cocoa ended nine higher at 936 stg per tonne, with traders eyeing stronger New York trade and possible gyrations in sterling after Britain's November budget.
Lacking fresh fundamental news, cocoa has been affected recently by sterling-related factors.
CBOT wheat futures were lower despite a more optimistic outlook for U.S. wheat exports.

Bangladesh, Pakistan, Sri Lanka and the Philippines were tendering for wheat and there were strong indications the United States would land most of the business, traders said. But buying was affected by concerns about a drop early in the Dow.
IPE Brent futures rebounded after slumping sharply on Monday on news of the Iraq-U.N. oil-for-food deal.
